effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive census percentages and institutional case-study findings only; no inferential statistical model, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported, and the author explicitly notes on PDF p. 9 that the descriptive analysis does not control for confounding factors so causality cannot be firmly attributed to privatization.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive INEGI census comparisons (1990–2010; Table 3) show that in the privatized Distrito Federal (DF), basic household water network access changed from 96.7% (1990) to 97.9% (2005) and 97.7% (2010) (1.0% 20-year growth), while in-home piped connections rose from 69.4% (1990) to 85.1% (2005) and 86.5% (2010) (24.6% 20-year growth), compared with higher 20-year growth rates in publicly served Outer ZMCM (basic access 90.3% to 96.4%, +6.8%; in-home piped 52.4% to 74.1%, +41.4%), Outer ZMVM (basic access 86.0% to 95.7%, +11.3%; in-home piped 33.4% to 44.7%, +33.8%), and Mexico nationally (basic access 79.2% to 90.9%, +14.8%; in-home piped 48.4% to 67.7%, +39.9%). Qualitatively and from secondary reports, initial 10-year service concessions (1994–2003) connected roughly 90% of DF households to meters by 2002 and raised utility revenue collection by ~70% (1992–2001), whereas post-2003 opaque contract renegotiations, mayoral political manoeuvring, and lack of regional coordination coincided with customer-registry/metering backlogs, stalled network extension in poor boroughs, and temporary April 2009 service shutoffs affecting ~5 million residents; in 2011, civil society coalition COMDA used the 2002 Federal Transparency Law to secure SACM transparency commitments on rates, concessionaires, and water quality (no inferential statistical test, CI, or p-value reported).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 under the CODEBOOK.md §9 design ceiling (cannot exceed 2 for Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework). The empirical link between service-concession governance and household water access rests on aggregate descriptive census comparisons (Table 3) and secondary audit/press accounts (plus 3 personal communications confirming contract renewal delays), while post-2003 contract terms remained undisclosed and the author explicitly notes it is unclear whether access changes are attributable to privatization.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines 4-zone concession service boundaries vs surrounding municipalities (service_area), exclusion of the public from utility planning and national water planning (planning), flat vs graduated/income-differentiated tariffs and user-fee transparency (fees), metering/customer-registry backlogs and indefinitely delayed long-term contract renewals (delay), executive/utility opacity and policy reversals over contract extensions (discretion), individual complaints and COMDA's formal appeal to the DF Institute of Access to Information under the 2002 Federal Transparency Law (complaint, administrative_review), absence of public participation and civil-society mobilization (participation), overlapping/conflicting agencies across DF and State of Mexico jurisdictions (institutional_fragmentation), and municipal-national partisan manoeuvring and lack of regional coordination (political_coordination).
